title: Tenali Raman Tale 93

full_text:
A wealthy, vain merchant named Lakshmipati hosted a grand feast for the city councilors of Vijayanagara. To display his immense wealth, he served each guest with a spoon cast in solid gold.
Throughout the dinner, Lakshmipati repeatedly reminded his guests:
'Look at the golden spoons! Was there ever such magnificence? Eating with pure gold purifies the soul and elevates the flavor of the food!'

Tenali Raman sat quietly, eating his rice and lentil dal.
As the feast concluded, Tenali picked up his golden spoon, wiped it clean with his linen napkin, and deliberately slipped it into the inner pocket of his coat before the eyes of the host!

Lakshmipati was horrified: 'Tenali! Thou hast stolen my golden spoon! Put it back immediately!'

Tenali looked astonished:
'Stolen? Why, noble Lakshmipati! Didst thou not declare that eating with gold purifies the soul and elevates the food?
My poor digestion has been troubled for years; I thought that keeping this golden spoon near my stomach would cure my liver!'

Lakshmipati grew furious:
'Tenali, stop this ridiculous nonsense! A golden spoon is made of heavy metal; it cannot cure a sick stomach! Its only value is that it costs fifty gold dinars!'

Tenali smiled with penetrating wisdom:
'Aha! Then why didst thou boast for three hours that the spoon possessed magical spiritual virtue?
A golden spoon cannot make sour curry sweet, nor can it make a greedy man noble.
When a hungry beggar eats simple porridge with his fingers with a clean heart, his meal is blessed; but when a vain man eats with a golden spoon while despising the poor, his gold is only heavy dirt.'

Tenali placed the golden spoon back upon the silver platter.
Lakshmipati lowered his eyes in shame, recognizing that true nobility is found in generous hospitality, not in ostentatious cutlery.
moral: True nourishment comes from honest food, not from the golden utensils that carry it.
